events_chronological: At a girls' day school, a mistress takes charge of a set of ten-year-olds and informs them that she is in her prime.
She teaches them about her dead fiance, about Italian painting and about her own opinions, in place of the syllabus.
She walks the set through the old part of the city and halts them in front of a queue of unemployed men.
The headmistress tries repeatedly to force her resignation and can find no grounds for it.
The art master, who has one arm, a wife and six children, kisses her in the art room.
She gives him up and takes the singing master as her lover instead.
She spends her weekends at the singing master's house on the coast with two of the girls attending as chaperones.
She decides that one particular girl shall become the art master's lover in her place.
The set's dull one, whom everybody blames for everything, leaves the school.
A different girl becomes the art master's lover, and discovers that every portrait he paints of any of them comes out looking like their teacher.
The mistress encourages a new girl to run away and fight in a foreign war.
The new girl is killed when her train is attacked, having gone to fight for the wrong side.
The singing master marries the science mistress.
The girl who became the art master's lover tells the headmistress that their teacher instructs in fascism, and hands her the grounds she has wanted for years.
The mistress is forced into retirement and spends the rest of her life trying to work out which of the set betrayed her.
The dull one dies at twenty-three in a hotel fire, running the wrong way along a corridor.
The mistress dies of an internal growth, and her betrayer, now an enclosed nun who has written a book on psychology, is asked through the grille what the chief influences of her schooldays were.
nonlinear_category_reason: The schooldays run forward, and the narration keeps splicing in real later scenes - a former pupil's death in a fire, another's life as a nun - decades ahead of where the story has reached.
syuzhet_notes: The narration keeps interrupting the school years to state and then stage what becomes of the girls, so one pupil's death in a hotel fire and another's life behind a convent grille arrive long before the years they follow. Both are given as scenes rather than merely foretold.
fabula_notes: The chronology of the school years is fixed by the girls' ages and by the foreign war the new girl runs off to. The two future scenes are dated by the ages the narration supplies.
